title: Trending — Educational expansion and the hidden reversal of the Flynn effect—Differential trends across socioeconomic strata
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
one_line: Using conscription cognitive tests linked to administrative registries for 579,379 Norwegian men across 25 birth cohorts (1967–1991), the authors show the Flynn effect reversed earlier in high-SES strata and was temporarily masked in lower strata by educational expansion.
key_claims: Sons of high-income fathers peaked in cognitive scores in late-1960s birth cohorts, while low-income strata peaked around mid-1970s cohorts — roughly a decade later — with smaller postpeak declines.
Opposing trends across income strata mathematically cancelled in the national average, producing a deceptively flat trend and hiding an earlier-onset population decline.

In a generalized additive change-on-change model within paternal-income percentiles, each additional year of schooling at conscription age was associated with about 4.2 IQ points, in line with quasi-experimental estimates (~1–5 points/year).
Adding years of education raised deviance explained from 6.4% (cohort and SES rank only) to 22.1%.

After Norway's 1994 high school reform and earlier expansions saturated upper-secondary attendance, the compensatory effect vanished and scores declined across all strata, most steeply among higher-income groups.
limitations: Cognitive data exist only at conscription age (~18–19), not early childhood, so reverse causality (higher-ability youths staying in school longer) cannot be fully excluded — acknowledged by the authors.
Sample is Norwegian men only, from conscription cohorts born 1967–1991, limiting generalisability to women and other countries.
SES was proxied by paternal income rank alone because rising female labour force participation made maternal/household income an unstable measure across these decades.
Confounder control relied on proxies — birth weight, gestational age, height at conscription, parental education — rather than direct measures of nutrition or prenatal environment.
The data identify that a broad decline is occurring but cannot identify its cause; affected subtests (math reasoning, word similarities) are schooling-sensitive crystallized abilities.
open_questions: Would childhood baseline cognitive measures linked to later schooling resolve the reverse-causality ambiguity in the ~4.2 points/year estimate?
Do the same SES-staggered peaks appear in other countries and in women, or is the pattern specific to Norway's education expansion timeline?
Does the post-plateau decline reflect real cognitive change or declining relevance of a decades-old military test to current learning environments?
What non-educational societal levers, if any, could reverse the decline now that secondary schooling is saturated?
